newsitem.title: USA: BASKETBALL-FIFTEEN NOMINEES ANNOUNCED FOR HALL OF FAME.
newsitem.headline: BASKETBALL-FIFTEEN NOMINEES ANNOUNCED FOR HALL OF FAME.

text.p: Alex English, who ranks seventh on the all-time NBA scoring list, and coaches Alex Hannum and Jerry Tarkanian are among 15 nominees for election to the Basketball Hall of Fame announced Tuesday.
The group of nominees featured seven players, seven coaches and one contributor.
Players nominated were English, Dennis Johnson, Gus Johnson, Bobby Jones, Sidney Moncrief, Jo Jo White and Jamaal Wilkes. English, Jones and Moncrief are first-time nominees.

Coaches nominated included Hannum, Tarkanian, Pete Carril, Don Haskins, Jim Phelan, John Thompson and Tex Winter along with contributor Lee Williams. Hannum is the only first-time nominee among the coaches.
Nominees from the Women's, Veterans and International Committees will be announced later this week.

An individual needs 18 of 24 votes from the Honours Committee for induction. New inductees will be announced on February 3, 1997, with enshrinement ceremonies to be held in Springfield on September 29.
English, an eight-time All-Star, was the first player in NBA history to score 2,000 points in eight straight seasons and ranks seventh all-time with 21,645 career points.
Dennis Johnson, a top defensive guard, was a starter for three NBA championship teams -- for Seattle in 1979 and the Boston Celtics in 1984 and 1986.

Gus Johnson, a four-time All-Star, was the prototype power forward in the 1960s and 1970s with the Baltimore Bullets. Twice voted to the NBA's All-Defensive First Team, he averaged 17.1 points and 12.7 rebounds in a nine seasons.
Jones, a four-time NBA All-Star with Denver and Philadelphia, was voted to the NBA's All-Defensive First Team eight consecutive years.
Moncrief was a five-time All-Star guard with the Milwaukee Bucks. The two-time NBA Defensive Player of the Year led the Bucks to seven straight Central Division titles.
White, a seven-time NBA All-Star, was a starting guard on two Celtic championship teams and was named MVP of the 1976 NBA Finals.

Wilkes, a three-time NBA All-Star, was a starting forward on four NBA championship teams (Golden State in 1975, Los Angeles Lakers in 1980, 1982, and 1985). Wilkes also won NCAA titles at UCLA in 1972 and 1973.
Hannum is the only coach to win an NBA title and an ABA championship. He coached the Philadelphia Warriors to the 1967 NBA championship and the Oakland Oaks to the 1969 ABA title.
Tarkanian has the best winning percentage of any college coach (.826) and has 647 victories. Tarkanian, now head coach at Fresno State, led Nevada-Las Vegas to the 1990 NCAA title.
Carril led Princeton to 514 wins in 29 seasons, including 13 Ivy League titles. He coached the Tigers to ten 20 plus-win seasons, 13 postseason appearances and the 1975 NIT title.
Haskins, head coach at Texas-El Paso, is tied for fifth on the NCAA's all-time win list with a 678-313 record. He won the 1966 NCAA title with the first all-black championship team.
Phelan has coached Mount St. Mary's for 42 seasons and his 758 wins ranks him second among active coaches. He made five trips to the NCAA Division II Final Four with a title in 1962.
Thompson led Georgetown to the 1984 NCAA title, NCAA Final Fours in 1982, 1984 and 1985 and 14 consecutive NCAA tournament appearances. He owns a 553-208 career record.
Winter, a veteran of 49 coaching seasons, was an assistant on four NBA title teams with the Chicago Bulls. He led Kansas State to eight Big Eight championships and four Final Fours.
Williams, former chief of the Hall of Fame, helped in creating the first Hall on the Springfield College campus in 1968 and then in the building of a new museum in 1985.
